title: Nature Data Tracker
goal: Your kid picks one thing in nature that changes every day, like the temperature, the rain or the sunset time, and tracks it for one or two weeks. They record real numbers, work out the daily changes, chart them, find the trend and use it to predict what comes next. It's what forecasters do, with a window and a notebook.
need: A notebook, or a note on a phone
Something to measure with: an outdoor thermometer, a clear straight-sided jar and a ruler for rain, or sunset times from a weather app
A set spot to check from: a window, a porch, a yard
Two minutes at the same time every day

lesson.text: One day doesn't make a trend. Compare averages, not single days, to see where the numbers are really going.
lesson.before: Today was colder than yesterday, so it's getting colder.

model.line: It's warming up by about 2.6°, even with a few colder days in the middle.

lesson.modelNote: That's the thinking this guide builds: look past the daily bumps to the bigger direction.

academics.subject: Math
academics.text: differences, averages, reading and making charts

academics.subject: Reasoning
academics.text: making a prediction and testing it

howTo.intro: You don't need teaching experience. You keep it short and steady; they collect the data. Two minutes at the same time each day is plenty. Don't point out the pattern. After a few days, ask what they notice.

plan.what: Pick what to track, set it up and start the routine (Steps 1 and 2).
Guess, check, record and work out the change (Steps 2 and 3).
Chart it, find the trend, then predict and check (Steps 4 and 5).

troubleshoot.a: Leave a gap in the log and keep going. Real scientists have missing data too. It's a good talk about why gaps matter.
Record them anyway. A flat stretch is part of the pattern. Or add a second thing to track that moves more, like rain.

skills.name: Consistency
skills.text: same time, same place, every day

steps.title: Pick what to track and set it up
steps.why: The best thing to track has a clear number and changes a little every day.
steps.kid: Your kid picks one thing to measure: the temperature at one time each day, the rain in a jar, the sunset time, the birds at a feeder. Then they set it up: a thermometer in the shade, a rain gauge made from a straight-sided jar and a ruler, or a weather app for sunset times.
steps.you: Help them pick something easy to check at the same time every day. 'The temperature after breakfast' gives sharper data than 'the weather'.
ask: What changes outside that you could put a number on?
Why does the thermometer go in the shade, not the sun?
steps.tip: Building the rain gauge is a great first job: tape a ruler to the outside of a clear jar, with the zero at the bottom.

levels.explore: Pick something simple to notice, like sunny, cloudy or rainy.
levels.develop: Pick something with a real number, and set up the tool.
levels.extend: Pick two things to track at once, like temperature and sunset time.

steps.title: Guess, check, record
steps.why: Same time, same place, every day turns checks into data you can compare.
steps.kid: Your kid picks a check-in time and a spot they'll stick to. Every day, they guess today's number first, then check and record it in a log: the date, the guess and the real number. A week is the minimum, two weeks is better.
steps.you: Help them remember, and prompt the guess. Ask 'what might make you forget, and how can we fix that now?'
ask: What do you think today's number will be?
Was your guess too high or too low?
steps.tip: Tie the check to something that already happens every day, like breakfast or brushing teeth. The habit sticks much better.

levels.explore: Make a daily mark or symbol for a week, like a sun or a cloud.
levels.develop: Record a real number every day for a week, with a guess first.
levels.extend: Record for two weeks, and keep track of how close each guess was.

steps.title: Work out the daily changes
steps.why: The difference between days is where the story starts.
steps.kid: Next to each number, your kid writes the change from the day before: +3 for 3 degrees warmer, −2 for 2 millimetres less rain, +2 for a sunset 2 minutes later. Then they find the biggest jump and the smallest change.
steps.you: Keep the maths conversational, in real-life words: warmer by, colder by, later than. Ask 'how do you know?'
ask: Was today warmer or colder than yesterday, and by how much?
Which day had the biggest change?
steps.tip: Negative numbers show up naturally here. 'It went down by 4' is −4, and kids get it right away.

levels.explore: Say which day stood out, and whether it went up or down.
levels.develop: Work out the change from one day to the next for the whole week.
levels.extend: Find the biggest and smallest changes, and the typical change per day.

steps.title: Chart it and find the trend
steps.why: A chart makes the pattern jump off the page.
steps.kid: Your kid makes a simple chart: days along the bottom, the number up the side, a dot or a bar for each day. Then they look at the whole thing and decide: is it climbing, dropping or staying flat? They compare the average of the first few days with the average of the last few.
steps.you: Keep the chart simple. Let them find the trend before you say anything. Ask 'do any days break the pattern?'
ask: Is the line climbing, dropping or bumpy?
What's the average of your first 3 days and your last 3 days?
steps.tip: Graph paper or a squared notebook makes the chart much easier, with one square for each degree or minute.

levels.explore: Make a simple bar or dot chart and say if it went up or down.
levels.develop: Chart the data and describe the trend in one sentence.
levels.extend: Draw the average line, mark the days far from it, and explain why they might be odd.

steps.title: Predict and check
steps.why: A forecaster's payoff: using the trend to see ahead.
steps.kid: Using the trend, your kid predicts the next few days and writes each prediction with a reason: 'Sunset will keep getting about 2 minutes earlier each day.' Then they keep tracking and check. Were they right, close or way off?
steps.you: Treat their prediction like a real forecast. A miss is a great result: 'why didn't it go the way the pattern said?' is the best question in the guide.
ask: What will tomorrow's number be, and why?
steps.tip: Race their forecast against a weather app for a few days. Kids love beating the app, even once.

levels.explore: Guess whether tomorrow goes up or down, then check.
levels.develop: Predict tomorrow's number with a reason, then check it.
levels.extend: Forecast 3 days ahead, then work out how far off each prediction was.

after.label: The tracker maths
lines: Prediction = last number + typical daily change

conclusion.headline: The numbers told a story.
conclusion.text: Your kid collected real data, tracked it every day, worked out the changes, charted it, found the trend and used it to see ahead. Differences, averages and charts, about the real world outside the window.
conclusion.celebrate: Ask them to explain the chart to someone else in the family: what it shows, and what they predict next.
extensions: Keep one tracker going for a whole month and watch a bigger trend appear
Track two things at once and see if their lines rise and fall together
Compare your data with a friend's in another city
Track the same thing again in a different season and compare

signs: They guess the temperature before checking
They notice the days getting longer or shorter
They ask 'is that a trend or just one day?'
makeItReal: Put the log somewhere everyone sees it, like the fridge or the door. When the whole family checks the numbers and asks about the trend, your kid becomes the house forecaster.
levelsLine: Every step has three levels: Explore, Develop, Extend. Pick the one that fits your kid today, and change it anytime. Siblings can do the same step at different levels, side by side.
